q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000 and its average creditors are Rs 2,25,000. The creditors turnover ratio is:
e: Creditors turnover ratio = Annual credit purchases/Average creditors = Rs 18,00,000/Rs 2,25,000 = 8 times.

q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 21,60,000 and its average creditors are Rs 2,70,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average payment period is:
e: Average payment period = 360/Creditors turnover = 360 x Rs 2,70,000/Rs 21,60,000 = 45 days.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 3/15, net 60. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of forgoing the discount = (3/97) x (360/(60 - 15)) = 3.09% x 8 = 24.7% approximately per annum, far above normal borrowing rates, so the discount should be taken.

q: 'Forfaiting', as a technique of financing receivables, refers to:

options.A: Selling the receivables to a factor with full recourse to the seller
options.B: The purchase, without recourse, of export receivables (such as bills of exchange or promissory notes) by a forfaiter, who assumes the credit and country risks for a discount
options.C: Writing off irrecoverable debts at the end of the year
options.D: Insuring the receivables against loss through an insurance company

e: Forfaiting is the purchase, without recourse to the exporter, of export receivables such as bills of exchange or promissory notes by a forfaiter, who takes over the credit and country risks for a discount.

q: When the receivables of a firm are 'pledged' as security for a loan:

options.A: The receivables are sold outright to the lender
options.B: No loan can be raised against receivables in any circumstances
options.C: The customers are invariably directed to pay the lender from the very beginning
options.D: The firm retains the ownership of the receivables but assigns them as collateral; on the firm's default, the lender may collect the receivables to recover the loan

e: When receivables are pledged, the firm keeps ownership of them but assigns them as collateral for the loan; only on default can the lender collect the receivables to recover the loan.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 36,00,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 60 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 12% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2AT/i) = sqrt(2 x Rs 36,00,000 x Rs 60/0.12) = sqrt(3,60,00,00,000) = Rs 60,000, balancing transaction cost against opportunity (interest) cost.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 15,000 and a spread of Rs 90,000 between the control limits. The return point (target cash balance) is:
e: In the Miller-Orr model, the return point = lower limit + one-third of the spread = Rs 15,000 + (Rs 90,000/3) = Rs 15,000 + Rs 30,000 = Rs 45,000.

q: In cash management, the 'net float' of a firm at a point of time is:

options.A: The total value of cheques deposited by the firm during a month
options.B: The excess of disbursement (payment) float over collection float — where it is positive, the bank balance exceeds the book balance because cheques issued have not yet been presented for payment
options.C: The cash kept in the office safe for emergencies
options.D: The portion of the sanctioned overdraft limit not yet utilised

e: Net float is disbursement float minus collection float; when positive, cheques issued but not yet presented make the bank balance higher than the book (ledger) balance of the firm.

q: A 'zero-balance account' system of cash management works by:

options.A: Keeping the master bank account of the enterprise permanently at a zero balance
options.B: Maintaining the accounts of the enterprise with one bank only
options.C: Closing all the bank accounts at the end of the financial year
options.D: Maintaining disbursement (sub) accounts at a zero balance, funds being transferred from the master concentration account exactly as and when the cheques presented are paid, so that no idle balances lie in the sub-accounts

e: In a zero-balance system, disbursement sub-accounts are kept at zero and funds are transferred from the master concentration account only when cheques are actually presented, so no idle balances lie in the sub-accounts.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 13,50,000 on capital employed of Rs 90,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: Return on Investment = Profit/Capital employed x 100 = Rs 13,50,000/Rs 90,00,000 x 100 = 15%.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 15,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 1,00,00,000. The cost of capital is 13%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = Profit - (cost of capital x capital employed) = Rs 15,00,000 - (13% x Rs 1,00,00,000) = Rs 15,00,000 - Rs 13,00,000 = Rs 2,00,000.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) of a division is Rs 18,00,000, its capital employed is Rs 1,20,00,000 and the cost of capital is 11%. Its Economic Value Added (EVA) is:
e: EVA = NOPAT - (cost of capital x capital employed) = Rs 18,00,000 - (11% x Rs 1,20,00,000) = Rs 18,00,000 - Rs 13,20,000 = Rs 4,80,000.

q: A selling division is working at full capacity and can sell its entire output in the outside market. The minimum transfer price it should charge for a component transferred internally is:

options.A: The variable cost per unit only
options.B: Nil, since the transfer is internal to the enterprise
options.C: The full absorption cost per unit only
options.D: The variable cost per unit plus the contribution lost on the outside sales forgone (opportunity cost), which is effectively the market price

e: At full capacity, every unit transferred internally sacrifices an outside sale, so the minimum transfer price = variable cost + contribution lost on the forgone outside sales, which works out to the market price.

q: Which of the following measures belongs to the 'internal business process' perspective of the Balanced Scorecard?

options.A: Manufacturing cycle time and the percentage of defective output

e: Manufacturing cycle time and the percentage of defective output measure how well the firm's operations run, so they belong to the internal business process perspective; the other options belong to the customer, financial and learning perspectives respectively.

q: The Balanced Scorecard framework was developed by:

options.C: Robert S. Kaplan and David P. Norton

e: The Balanced Scorecard, which translates strategy into financial, customer, internal process and learning measures, was developed by Robert S. Kaplan and David P. Norton.

q: A distinguishing feature of the management audit report, as compared with the statutory audit report, is that:

options.A: It is never submitted in writing
options.B: It has no prescribed or standard format, and it covers suggestions for improvement of policies, organisation and performance, besides reporting weaknesses
options.C: It must be published in the newspapers for the information of the public
options.D: It is addressed to the shareholders in general meeting

e: Unlike the statutory audit report, the management audit report has no prescribed format; besides reporting weaknesses, it suggests improvements in policies, organisation and performance for management's consideration.

q: The expected market price of a product is Rs 1,250 per unit and the firm desires a profit of 25% on cost. The target cost of the product is:
e: Target cost = market price - desired profit. Profit is 25% on cost, so price = 125% of cost and target cost = Rs 1,250/1.25 = Rs 1,000.

q: A product gives a throughput of Rs 750 per unit and takes 0.25 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. The return per factory (bottleneck) hour is:
e: Return per factory hour = throughput per unit/bottleneck time per unit = Rs 750/0.25 hour = Rs 3,000 per bottleneck hour, the throughput accounting measure for ranking products.

q: Kaizen costing differs from standard costing mainly in that:

options.A: It is applied before the production of the product begins
options.B: It assumes that costs can be improved only by a complete redesign of the product
options.C: It sets explicit cost-reduction targets for each period during the manufacturing phase, and the workers continually seek small improvements to achieve them, instead of merely maintaining the existing cost standards
options.D: It ignores the actual costs incurred during the period

e: Kaizen costing works during the manufacturing phase: explicit cost-reduction targets are set for each period and workers continually make small improvements to meet them, unlike standard costing, which mainly maintains existing standards.

q: 'Terotechnology', a concept closely associated with life-cycle costing, is concerned with:

options.A: The study of land and buildings only
options.B: The pursuit of the economic life-cycle cost of physical assets through a combination of engineering, financial and managerial techniques covering their installation, operation, maintenance and disposal
options.C: Insurance of assets against terrorist attacks
options.D: The technique of raising term loans for plant and machinery

e: Terotechnology applies engineering, financial and managerial techniques together to pursue the lowest economic life-cycle cost of physical assets over their installation, operation, maintenance and disposal.

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 3,00,000 when the general price index stood at 120. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 180. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
e: CPP restated value = historical cost x (current index/index at purchase) = Rs 3,00,000 x 180/120 = Rs 4,50,000, expressing the asset in current purchasing power units.

q: In Current Cost Accounting (CCA), the Monetary Working Capital Adjustment (MWCA) is made in order to:

options.A: Recognise the effect of changes in the specific prices of inputs on the monetary working capital (net trade debtors and creditors), representing the additional finance needed to maintain the same operating capability
options.B: Restate the debtors and creditors at their market values at the balance-sheet date
options.C: Write off the bad and doubtful debts of the enterprise
options.D: Convert foreign-currency monetary items at the closing exchange rate

e: The MWCA recognises how specific price changes affect monetary working capital (net trade debtors less creditors): extra finance is needed to maintain the same operating capability, and this adjustment charges that effect.

q: The 'gearing adjustment' in Current Cost Accounting (CCA):

options.A: Adjusts the depreciation charge of the year for price changes
options.B: Restates the opening balance sheet of the enterprise at current costs
options.C: Abates (reduces) the total of the depreciation, cost of sales and monetary working capital adjustments to the extent that the operating assets are financed by lenders (net borrowings) rather than by the shareholders, the benefit being credited to the profit and loss account
options.D: Is applicable only to government companies and departmental undertakings

e: The gearing adjustment abates the depreciation, cost of sales and MWCA adjustments in proportion to net borrowings, because part of the operating assets is financed by lenders; the gearing benefit is credited to the profit and loss account.

q: Under the 'opportunity cost approach' to human resource accounting (proposed by Hekimian and Jones), the value of an employee is determined by:

options.A: The total earnings drawn by the employee in the past
options.B: Competitive bidding within the organisation — the divisions bid for the scarce employees, and the bid price forms the basis of the employee's capitalised value
options.C: The cost that would be incurred in replacing the employee
options.D: A standard table of values prescribed by the Government

e: Under the Hekimian and Jones opportunity cost approach, divisions bid competitively for scarce employees within the organisation, and the bid price forms the basis of the employee's capitalised value in human resource accounting.

q: A factory has 5,000 units of work-in-progress. The direct material cost is Rs 60 per unit and conversion costs of Rs 4,00,000 have also been incurred on this work-in-progress. Under throughput accounting, the value at which this inventory will be carried is:
e: Throughput accounting values inventory at material cost only, treating all conversion costs as period expenses: 5,000 units x Rs 60 = Rs 3,00,000. The Rs 4,00,000 conversion cost is not carried in inventory.

q: The works cost of a job is Rs 1,60,000. Office and administration overheads are 10% of works cost and selling and distribution overheads are Rs 24,000. If a profit of 25% on total cost is required, the tender (selling) price to be quoted is:
e: Total cost = works cost Rs 1,60,000 + office overheads 10% of works cost (Rs 16,000) + selling overheads Rs 24,000 = Rs 2,00,000. Tender price = Rs 2,00,000 + 25% profit = Rs 2,50,000.

q: The total cost of producing 4,000 units is Rs 46,000 and that of producing 7,000 units is Rs 64,000. Using the high-low method, the fixed cost is:
Carriage outward, incurred on delivering finished goods to customers, is classified in cost accounts as:

options.C: A direct expense forming part of prime cost

e: Carriage outward is incurred after production, in delivering finished goods to customers, so it is a selling and distribution overhead, not a factory overhead or part of prime cost.

q: A 'bill of materials' is:

options.A: A statement of the materials lying in the stores at the end of a period
options.B: A demand note sent by the stores to the purchase department
options.C: The invoice received from a supplier of materials
options.D: A complete schedule of all the materials and components, with quantities, required for a specified job or product, prepared in advance

e: A bill of materials is a complete schedule, prepared in advance, of all materials and components with quantities required for a specified job or product; it authorises the stores to issue those materials.

q: Materials issued for one job are found surplus on that job and are transferred directly to another job without being returned to the stores. The document used to record such a transfer is the:
e: Surplus material moved directly from one job to another without returning to stores is recorded on a material transfer note; a material return note is used only when material goes back into stores.

q: The opening stock of a material is 100 units at Rs 20 per unit. A further 200 units are purchased at Rs 24 per unit. If 180 units are issued, the value of the issue under the FIFO method is:
e: Under FIFO, the 180 units issued come first from the oldest lot: 100 units x Rs 20 + 80 units x Rs 24 = Rs 2,000 + Rs 1,920 = Rs 3,920.

q: Materials were purchased in three lots: 200 units at Rs 12, 100 units at Rs 15 and 100 units at Rs 18 per unit. The issue price under the simple average price method is:
e: Simple average price = (Rs 12 + Rs 15 + Rs 18)/3 = Rs 15 per unit. The simple average ignores the quantities bought in each lot, unlike the weighted average.

q: 'Defectives' in production are units which:

options.A: Are completely unsaleable and have no disposal value at all
options.B: Fall short of the quality standards and cannot be rectified at any cost
options.C: Are produced in excess of the quantity ordered by the customer
options.D: Do not conform to the prescribed standards of quality but can be rectified and brought up to standard by incurring additional expenditure on material, labour and overheads

e: Defectives fall short of quality standards but can be rectified and brought up to standard by spending extra on material, labour and overheads; units that are totally unsaleable are spoilage or scrap.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 500 units per week, the normal consumption is 350 units per week and the maximum lead time is 4 weeks. The safety stock is:
e: Safety stock = (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time = (500 - 350) x 4 = 150 x 4 = 600 units.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 12,800 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 50 and the carrying cost is Rs 2 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C) = sqrt(2 x 12,800 x 50/2) = sqrt(6,40,000) = 800 units.

q: Overtime is worked in a factory specifically at the request of a customer who wants his job completed ahead of schedule. In cost accounts, the overtime premium in such a case is:

options.A: Charged directly to that customer's job
options.C: Charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: Recovered from the workers who worked the overtime

e: Overtime premium worked at a customer's specific request for early completion is a direct charge to that customer's job, not general factory overhead, because the job alone caused the extra cost.

q: Which of the following is a 'preventive cost' of labour turnover?

options.A: Cost of recruiting and selecting replacement workers
options.B: Cost of training the new workers engaged
options.C: Loss of output during the learning period of new workers
options.D: Cost of providing safety measures, welfare amenities and good working conditions so as to retain the existing workforce

e: Preventive costs of labour turnover are incurred to retain the existing workforce - safety measures, welfare amenities and good working conditions. Recruitment, training and learning-period losses arise after turnover and are replacement costs.

q: A worker is paid a piece rate of Rs 15 per unit, subject to a guaranteed minimum wage of Rs 3,200 per week. If he produces 240 units in a week, his total earnings for the week are:
e: Piece wages = 240 units x Rs 15 = Rs 3,600, which exceeds the guaranteed minimum of Rs 3,200, so the worker is paid Rs 3,600.

q: Under the Halsey-Weir premium plan, a worker receives a bonus of 30% of the wages of the time saved. A worker is allowed 20 hours for a job, completes it in 16 hours and is paid at Rs 75 per hour. His total earnings are:
e: Time wages = 16 hours x Rs 75 = Rs 1,200. Time saved = 4 hours; bonus = 30% of wages of time saved = 30% x (4 x Rs 75) = Rs 90. Total earnings = Rs 1,200 + Rs 90 = Rs 1,290.

q: The expenses of the factory canteen are apportioned among the production and service departments on the basis of:

options.A: The number of workers employed in each department
options.B: The floor area occupied by each department
options.C: The direct wages paid in each department
options.D: The value of materials issued to each department

e: Canteen expenses serve the workers, so they are apportioned among departments on the basis of the number of workers employed in each department.

q: In cost accounting, 'allocation' of an item of cost refers to:

options.A: Apportioning a common cost among cost centres on an equitable basis
options.B: Absorbing overheads into the cost of products
options.C: Distributing the costs of service departments to production departments
options.D: Charging the whole of an item of cost directly to a single cost centre or cost unit with which it is exclusively identified, without any apportionment

e: Allocation means charging the whole of a cost item directly to the single cost centre or cost unit with which it is exclusively identified, with no apportionment; shared costs, by contrast, are apportioned on an equitable basis.

q: The machine hour rate method of absorbing factory overheads is most suitable in a department where:

options.A: Production is carried out mainly by manual labour
options.B: Production is highly machine-based and machines are the predominant factor of production
options.C: Only one single product is manufactured
options.D: Overheads consist mainly of indirect wages

e: The machine hour rate suits a department where production is highly machine-based and machines predominate, because overheads there vary more closely with machine hours than with labour.

q: Budgeted factory overheads are Rs 3,60,000 and the budgeted direct material cost is Rs 6,00,000. Overheads are absorbed as a percentage of direct material cost. A job whose direct material cost is Rs 40,000 will absorb factory overheads of:
e: Absorption rate = Rs 3,60,000/Rs 6,00,000 = 60% of direct material cost. Overheads absorbed by the job = 60% x Rs 40,000 = Rs 24,000.

q: Budgeted factory overheads are Rs 4,80,000 and the budgeted output is 60,000 units, giving a predetermined absorption rate per unit. Actual output is 55,000 units and actual overheads incurred are Rs 4,60,000. The overheads are:
e: Predetermined rate = Rs 4,80,000/60,000 = Rs 8 per unit. Absorbed = 55,000 x Rs 8 = Rs 4,40,000 against actual Rs 4,60,000, so overheads are under-absorbed by Rs 20,000.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 2,40,000. Production is 30,000 units and sales are 27,000 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing will be:
e: Fixed overhead rate = Rs 2,40,000/30,000 units = Rs 8 per unit. Production exceeds sales by 3,000 units, so Rs 24,000 of fixed overhead is carried in closing stock under absorption costing, making its profit higher by Rs 24,000.

q: Under marginal costing, for a given selling price and cost structure, the profit of a period is determined by:

options.A: The volume of production of the period
options.B: The volume of sales of the period, since the fixed costs are charged in full against the revenue of the period
options.C: The volume of closing stock of finished goods
options.D: The method adopted for valuing work-in-progress

e: Under marginal costing, fixed costs are charged in full to the period, so profit depends on the volume of sales, not production; extra production merely builds stock valued at variable cost.

q: A product sells for Rs 175 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 105 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 2,80,000 and 6,000 units are sold. The profit under marginal costing is:
e: Contribution = (Rs 175 - Rs 105) x 6,000 units = Rs 4,20,000. Profit = contribution - fixed costs = Rs 4,20,000 - Rs 2,80,000 = Rs 1,40,000.

q: A product sells for Rs 320 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 200 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: Break-even point = Fixed costs/Contribution per unit = Rs 3,60,000/(Rs 320 - Rs 200) = Rs 3,60,000/Rs 120 = 3,000 units.

q: The P/V ratio of a firm is 45%. If its sales increase by Rs 2,00,000, with no change in fixed costs or the P/V ratio, its profit will increase by:
e: With fixed costs and the P/V ratio unchanged, extra profit = extra sales x P/V ratio = Rs 2,00,000 x 45% = Rs 90,000.

q: A firm sells 40,000 units in a period and its break-even point is 28,000 units. Its margin of safety in units is:
e: Margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales = 40,000 - 28,000 = 12,000 units, the amount by which sales can fall before losses begin.

q: An enterprise wants to earn a profit after tax of Rs 1,20,000. The tax rate is 20%, fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000 and the P/V ratio is 50%. The sales required are:
e: Required profit before tax = Rs 1,20,000/(1 - 0.20) = Rs 1,50,000. Required sales = (Fixed costs + required profit)/P/V ratio = (Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 1,50,000)/50% = Rs 7,00,000.

q: Labour hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 72 per unit and requires 3 labour hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 110 per unit and requires 5 labour hours per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per labour hour (Rs 24) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Product B, because it uses more labour hours per unit

e: Contribution per labour hour: A = Rs 72/3 = Rs 24; B = Rs 110/5 = Rs 22. With labour hours limiting, A earns more per scarce hour, so A gets production priority.

q: A factory has 20,000 kg of a scarce material. Product A, which ranks first on the basis of contribution per kg of material, requires 4 kg per unit and its maximum demand is 3,000 units. Product B requires 5 kg per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:
e: Product A uses 3,000 units x 4 kg = 12,000 kg. Material left = 20,000 - 12,000 = 8,000 kg, giving B = 8,000/5 kg = 1,600 units.

q: A factory has 6,000 machine hours available. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 50 per unit, requires 2 machine hours per unit and has a maximum demand of 2,000 units. Product B gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and requires 5 machine hours per unit. Contribution per machine hour ranks A first. The maximum total contribution obtainable is:
e: Contribution per machine hour: A = Rs 25, B = Rs 18, so A first: 2,000 units use 4,000 hours giving Rs 1,00,000. Remaining 2,000 hours make 400 units of B giving Rs 36,000. Total = Rs 1,36,000.

q: A firm requires 12,000 units of a component every year. Making it involves a variable cost of Rs 28 per unit and specific fixed costs of Rs 36,000 per year, which would be wholly avoided if the component were bought. An outside supplier offers it at Rs 33 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Buy, because the supplier's price is a firm quoted price per unit
options.B: Buy, because the fixed costs of making should be ignored altogether in the decision
options.C: Make, because the total relevant cost of making (Rs 3,72,000) is less than the cost of buying (Rs 3,96,000)
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the two alternatives cost the same

e: Relevant cost of making = variable cost (12,000 x Rs 28 = Rs 3,36,000) + avoidable specific fixed cost Rs 36,000 = Rs 3,72,000, against buying cost 12,000 x Rs 33 = Rs 3,96,000. Making is cheaper, so make.

q: A firm has spare capacity. Its variable cost is Rs 85 per unit. It receives a one-time special order for 1,500 units at Rs 95 per unit. Accepting the order requires special packing costing Rs 6 per unit, but involves no additional fixed cost. The order should be:

options.A: Accepted, because it yields an incremental gain of Rs 6,000
options.B: Rejected, because the price offered is below the normal selling price
options.C: Accepted only if the packing cost is borne by the buyer
options.D: Rejected, because it yields no gain at all

e: Incremental gain = 1,500 units x (Rs 95 - Rs 85 variable cost - Rs 6 packing) = 1,500 x Rs 4 = Rs 6,000. With spare capacity and no extra fixed cost, the order should be accepted.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 7,50,000 per year, of which Rs 3,00,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. Shutdown (discontinuance) costs of Rs 60,000 would also be incurred if the plant is closed. The contribution is Rs 51 per unit. The shutdown point is:
e: Shutdown point = (avoidable fixed costs + shutdown costs)/contribution per unit = (Rs 7,50,000 - Rs 3,00,000 + Rs 60,000)/Rs 51 = Rs 5,10,000/Rs 51 = 10,000 units; below this output, shutting down is cheaper.

q: A division earns a contribution of Rs 2,20,000. Its specific (avoidable) fixed costs are Rs 1,60,000, and common fixed costs of Rs 90,000 allocated to it would continue even if it were closed. If the division is closed down, the total profit of the company will:
e: Closing the division loses its contribution of Rs 2,20,000 but saves only the avoidable fixed costs of Rs 1,60,000 (the Rs 90,000 common costs continue), so company profit decreases by Rs 60,000.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 30 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 33 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 1,500 kg. The material price variance is:
e: Material price variance = (Standard price - Actual price) x Actual quantity = (Rs 30 - Rs 33) x 1,500 kg = Rs 4,500 (Adverse), because the actual price exceeds the standard.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 3,000 hours at a standard rate of Rs 50 per hour. Actual hours paid for are 3,300, out of which 200 hours were lost as idle time. The idle time variance is:
e: Idle time variance = idle hours x standard rate = 200 hours x Rs 50 = Rs 10,000 (Adverse); idle time is paid for but produces nothing.

q: The standard variable overhead rate is Rs 11 per hour and the standard time for the actual output is 5,500 hours. Actual variable overheads incurred are Rs 66,000. The variable overhead cost variance is:
e: Variable overhead cost variance = standard cost for actual output - actual cost = (5,500 hours x Rs 11) - Rs 66,000 = Rs 60,500 - Rs 66,000 = Rs 5,500 (Adverse).

q: Budgeted fixed overheads of a factory are Rs 1,80,000 and actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 1,92,000. The standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 8 per unit and actual production is 22,500 units. The fixed overhead cost (total) variance is:
e: Fixed overhead absorbed = 22,500 units x Rs 8 = Rs 1,80,000 against actual fixed overheads of Rs 1,92,000, so the fixed overhead cost variance = Rs 12,000 (Adverse).

q: The standard mix for a batch of 100 kg is: Material A — 40 kg at Rs 12 per kg, Material B — 60 kg at Rs 8 per kg. The actual mix used for a 100 kg batch is A — 50 kg and B — 50 kg. The material mix variance is:
e: Comparing actual mix with the standard mix at standard prices: A: (40 - 50) kg x Rs 12 = Rs 120 (Adverse); B: (60 - 50) kg x Rs 8 = Rs 80 (Favourable). Net mix variance = Rs 40 (Adverse).

q: In a process, 3,000 units are introduced and the normal loss is 10% of the input. The actual output obtained is 2,760 units. The abnormal gain is:
e: Expected output after normal loss = 3,000 - 10% x 3,000 = 2,700 units. Actual output is 2,760 units, so abnormal gain = 2,760 - 2,700 = 60 units.

q: In a process, 6,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process. The closing work-in-progress is 2,000 units, complete as to materials but only 50% complete as to conversion costs. The equivalent production in respect of conversion costs is:
e: Equivalent production for conversion costs = completed units 6,000 + (closing WIP 2,000 x 50% complete) = 6,000 + 1,000 = 7,000 units.

q: Process costing is the appropriate method of costing in industries where:

options.A: Each job is executed strictly to a customer's specific order
options.B: Services are rendered to customers, as in transport and hospital undertakings
options.C: Production is continuous, the product is homogeneous and the output of one process becomes the input of the next, as in cement, chemicals and oil refining
options.D: Identical units are produced in separate batches, each batch being a cost unit

e: Process costing suits continuous, mass production of homogeneous units where output flows through successive processes, each process's output becoming the next process's input - as in cement, chemicals and oil refining.

q: A hospital incurs total operating costs of Rs 18,00,000 during a period in which the total number of patient-days is 30,000. The operating cost per patient-day is:
e: Operating cost per patient-day = total operating cost/patient-days = Rs 18,00,000/30,000 = Rs 60, the service (operating) costing unit for a hospital.

q: Under activity-based costing, the machine maintenance cost pool of a plant is Rs 5,60,000 and the total maintenance hours in the period are 7,000. A product which requires 900 maintenance hours will be assigned maintenance cost of:
e: Activity rate = Rs 5,60,000/7,000 maintenance hours = Rs 80 per hour. Cost assigned = 900 hours x Rs 80 = Rs 72,000, using maintenance hours as the cost driver.

q: In activity-based costing, 'product-sustaining' (product-level) activities are activities which:

options.A: Are performed for each individual unit produced, such as machining a component
options.B: Are performed to support a particular product or product line as a whole — such as product design and engineering support — irrespective of how many units or batches of it are produced
options.C: Are performed each time a batch is processed, such as machine set-ups
options.D: Support the factory as a whole, such as plant security and management

e: Product-sustaining (product-level) activities support a particular product or product line as a whole - like product design and engineering support - and are performed regardless of how many units or batches are produced.

q: A material requisition note (store requisition) is:

options.A: A note prepared by the stores recording materials returned by a consuming department
options.B: A report of materials damaged or lost in the stores
options.C: A statement of all the materials required for a job, prepared in advance by the planning department
options.D: A document raised by the consuming department which authorises and requests the stores to issue the specified materials for a job or process

e: A material requisition note is raised by the consuming department to authorise and request the stores to issue the specified materials for a job or process; the storekeeper issues material only against it.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 15,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 4,00,000 at the end of each of the next 6 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 6 years at 10% is 4.355. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = (Rs 4,00,000 x 4.355) - Rs 15,00,000 = Rs 17,42,000 - Rs 15,00,000 = (+) Rs 2,42,000. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the 10% required return.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 8,00,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 10% = 0.909), Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 10% = 0.826) and Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 10% = 0.751). The Net Present Value of the project is:
A machine costing Rs 7,50,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 2,50,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = initial outlay/annual cash inflow = Rs 7,50,000/Rs 2,50,000 = 3 years, since the yearly inflows are uniform.

q: A project costing Rs 9,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,00,000 in Year 1, Rs 4,00,000 in Year 2 and Rs 4,00,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 2,00,000, Year 2 Rs 6,00,000. Balance of Rs 3,00,000 comes from Year 3's Rs 4,00,000, taking 9 months. Payback = 2 years 9 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 5,25,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 2, Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Cumulative discounted inflows: Year 1 Rs 2,50,000, Year 2 Rs 4,00,000, Year 3 Rs 5,00,000. The remaining Rs 25,000 comes from Year 4's Rs 1,00,000, taking 3 months. Discounted payback = 3 years 3 months.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 5,000 at a discount rate of 9% and (-) Rs 5,000 at a discount rate of 13%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: By interpolation, IRR = 9% + [5,000/(5,000 + 5,000)] x (13% - 9%) = 9% + 0.5 x 4% = 11%, the rate at which NPV becomes zero.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 4,25,000 and its initial investment is Rs 5,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = present value of future cash inflows/initial investment = Rs 4,25,000/Rs 5,00,000 = 0.85. Being below 1, it matches a negative NPV.

q: An investment of Rs 25,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 2,00,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: Average Rate of Return = average annual profit/initial investment x 100 = Rs 2,00,000/Rs 25,00,000 x 100 = 8%.

q: A project is expected to yield annual sales of Rs 5,00,000 and annual cash operating costs of Rs 3,00,000. Depreciation on the project assets is Rs 50,000 per year and the tax rate is 30%. The annual cash flow after tax from the project is:
e: Profit before tax = Rs 5,00,000 - Rs 3,00,000 - Rs 50,000 depreciation = Rs 1,50,000; tax at 30% = Rs 45,000; profit after tax = Rs 1,05,000. Adding back depreciation gives cash flow after tax = Rs 1,55,000.

q: When a proposed new product is expected to reduce the cash inflows from the enterprise's existing products, this effect (known as cannibalisation or erosion) should be treated in the capital budgeting appraisal of the new product as:

options.A: Ignored, since it does not involve any cash outlay
options.B: A benefit of the new product
options.C: A relevant cost (cash outflow) of the new product, since the loss of the existing cash inflows is an incremental effect of accepting it
options.D: A sunk cost of the existing products

e: Cannibalisation - the loss of cash inflows from existing products caused by the new product - is an incremental effect of accepting the new product, so it is a relevant cost in its appraisal.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of capital budgeting (capital expenditure) decisions?

options.A: They involve large outlays on long-term assets and are largely irreversible once taken
options.B: They can be reversed at any time without significant cost
options.C: They relate only to the day-to-day working capital of the enterprise
options.D: They are taken afresh every month as a matter of routine

e: Capital budgeting decisions commit large outlays to long-term assets and are largely irreversible once taken, which is why they need careful appraisal before funds are committed.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 10,00,000 (cost 12%), preference capital of Rs 4,00,000 (cost 9%) and debt of Rs 6,00,000 (after-tax cost 5%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 10% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 105 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of debt is:
e: Cost of debt = annual interest/issue proceeds = Rs 10/Rs 105 = 9.52%, since interest is paid on the face value of Rs 100 but the company receives Rs 105 per debenture.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 10 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 100 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 6% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = D1/P0 + g = (Rs 10/Rs 100 x 100) + 6% = 10% + 6% = 16%, by the dividend growth model.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 12% and the beta of the share is 2.0, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf) = 6% + 2.0 x (12% - 6%) = 6% + 12% = 18%. A beta of 2 doubles the market risk premium.

q: A share has a beta of 1.8. This indicates that:

options.A: The share is less risky than the market portfolio as a whole
options.B: The share tends to fluctuate more widely than the market as a whole, i.e., it is an aggressive share
options.C: The share carries no systematic risk at all
options.D: The share will earn exactly 1.8 times the risk-free rate

e: A beta of 1.8 means the share's returns tend to move 1.8 times as much as the market's: it fluctuates more widely than the market portfolio, making it an aggressive, high-systematic-risk share.

q: Under the 'pecking order' theory of financing, an enterprise generally prefers to raise funds in the order of:

options.A: New equity first, then debt, and internal accruals last
options.B: Debt first, then new equity, and internal accruals last
options.C: New equity first, then internal accruals, and debt last
options.D: Internal accruals (retained earnings) first, then debt, and new equity only as a last resort

e: The pecking order theory says firms prefer internal accruals (retained earnings) first, then debt, and issue new equity only as a last resort, because outside finance carries information and issue costs.

q: Under the Modigliani-Miller approach to dividend policy:

options.A: A higher dividend payout always increases the value of the firm
options.B: Dividend policy determines the capital structure of the firm
options.C: Dividend policy is irrelevant to the value of the firm, which depends on its earning power and investment policy
options.D: A firm should never pay any dividend to its shareholders

e: Under the Modigliani-Miller approach, dividend policy is irrelevant: the value of the firm depends on its earning power and investment policy, not on how earnings are split between dividends and retention.

q: Unlike interest on debt, the dividend on preference shares is not allowed as a deduction in computing the taxable income of a company because:

options.A: Preference dividend is an appropriation of profits, not a charge against profits
options.B: Preference shares are issued only at a premium
options.C: Preference dividend is paid only in profitable years
options.D: Preference dividend is paid out of the capital of the company

e: Preference dividend is an appropriation of after-tax profits, not a charge against profits like interest on debt, so it is not deductible in computing the company's taxable income.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 20,00,000, variable costs are Rs 11,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 4,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Contribution = Rs 20,00,000 - Rs 11,00,000 = Rs 9,00,000; EBIT = Rs 9,00,000 - Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000. Degree of operating leverage = Contribution/EBIT = 9,00,000/5,00,000 = 1.8.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 7,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 2,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT/(EBIT - Interest) = Rs 7,00,000/(Rs 7,00,000 - Rs 2,00,000) = 7,00,000/5,00,000 = 1.4.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 30,00,000, variable costs of Rs 18,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 4,00,000 and interest of Rs 3,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Contribution = Rs 30,00,000 - Rs 18,00,000 = Rs 12,00,000; EBT = Rs 12,00,000 - Rs 4,00,000 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000. Degree of combined leverage = Contribution/EBT = 12,00,000/5,00,000 = 2.4.

q: The degree of financial leverage of an enterprise is 1.6. If its earnings before interest and tax increase by 25%, its Earnings Per Share will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage change in EPS = DFL x percentage change in EBIT = 1.6 x 25% = 40%. Financial leverage magnifies the effect of an EBIT change on equity earnings.

q: A high degree of combined leverage in an enterprise indicates that:

options.A: The enterprise carries only business risk and no financial risk
options.B: The profits of the enterprise are completely stable
options.C: The enterprise uses no fixed-cost sources of finance
options.D: The enterprise is exposed to a high total risk, since the combined leverage magnifies the effect of changes in sales on the earnings per share

e: A high combined leverage means both fixed operating costs and fixed financial charges are heavy, so a change in sales is magnified all the way to EPS - the enterprise carries high total (combined) risk.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 19,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 10,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets/Current liabilities = Rs 19,00,000/Rs 10,00,000 = 1.9 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 16,50,000, including stock of Rs 5,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 1,00,000. Current liabilities are Rs 6,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = Rs 16,50,000 - stock Rs 5,00,000 - prepaid expenses Rs 1,00,000 = Rs 10,50,000. Quick ratio = Rs 10,50,000/Rs 6,00,000 = 1.75 : 1.

q: An enterprise has cash in hand of Rs 1,50,000, bank balance of Rs 1,00,000 and marketable securities of Rs 1,50,000. Its current liabilities are Rs 8,00,000. Its absolute liquid (super quick) ratio is:
e: Absolute liquid assets = cash Rs 1,50,000 + bank Rs 1,00,000 + marketable securities Rs 1,50,000 = Rs 4,00,000. Ratio = Rs 4,00,000/Rs 8,00,000 = 0.5 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 8,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 5,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt/Shareholders' funds = Rs 8,00,000/Rs 5,00,000 = 1.6 : 1.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 11,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 2,00,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = PBIT/Interest = Rs 11,00,000/Rs 2,00,000 = 5.5 times.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 3,60,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 60,000. If the equity shareholders' funds are Rs 12,00,000, the Return on Equity (return on equity shareholders' funds) is:
e: Return on Equity = (Net profit after tax - Preference dividend)/Equity shareholders' funds x 100 = (Rs 3,60,000 - Rs 60,000)/Rs 12,00,000 x 100 = 25%.
